kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-01.title: Check each picture for halves
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-01.body:
- (A): each grey triangle has a matching white triangle → grey = white.
- (B): two grey and two white triangles of the same size → equal.
- (C): 2 grey and 2 white small squares → equal.
- (E): the grey parts again make exactly half.
- (D): only **two small** grey triangles, each $\frac{1}{8}$ of the square, so grey $= \frac{1}{4}$ and white $= \frac{3}{4}$.

**Answer: (D)**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-01.title: Look at picture (D) closely
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-01.body:
The horizontal line cuts the square into two halves. The diagonal line cuts each half into a small triangle and a bigger piece. In each half only the small triangle (a quarter of that half) is grey. So the grey part is much smaller than the white part.

**Answer: (D)**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-02.title: List the different letters
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-02.body:
Write each letter only the first time it appears: M, A, T, H, E, I, C.

That is **7** different letters, so 7 colours.

**Answer: (A) 7**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-02.title: Count and remove repeats
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-02.body:
MATHEMATIC has 10 letters. M, A and T each appear twice, so there are 3 repeats: $10 - 3 = 7$.

**Answer: (A) 7**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-03.title: Neighbours share a peg
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-03.body:
Two towels next to each other share one peg. So there is one peg at the start and then one more peg after each towel: $1 + 5 = 6$.

**Answer: (C) 6**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-03.title: Continue the pattern
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-03.body:
1 towel → 2 pegs, 2 towels → 3 pegs, 3 towels → 4 pegs. Each new towel needs 1 more peg, so 4 towels → 5 pegs and 5 towels → 6 pegs.

**Answer: (C) 6**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-04.title: Use the whole column B
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-04.body:
B1, B2, B3 and B4 means the whole column B is coloured. Only grid (C) has all of column B grey. Check the rest of (C): A2 is grey, C3 and D3 are grey, D4 is grey — exactly the list.

**Answer: (C)**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-04.title: Rule out grids
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-04.body:
- (A) has C1 coloured, which is not in the list.
- (B) has B1 white.
- (D) has C1 and D1 coloured.
- (E) has B1 white.

Only (C) is left, and it matches all 8 fields.

**Answer: (C)**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-05.title: Take away the seeker first
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-05.body:
One child searches, so $13 - 1 = 12$ children hide. 9 of them are found: $12 - 9 = 3$ are still hiding.

**Answer: (A) 3**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-05.title: Add up
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-05.body:
Seeker + found + still hiding = 13, so $1 + 9 + ? = 13$, which gives $? = 3$.

**Answer: (A) 3**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-06.title: Add each score
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-06.body:
Mike's darts are in 25, 35 and 7: $25 + 35 + 7 = 67$.

Jake's darts are in 3, 15 and 45: $3 + 15 + 45 = 63$.

$67 - 63 = 4$, so Mike won by 4 points.

**Answer: (E)**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-06.title: Compare dart by dart
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-06.body:
Pair the darts: Mike's 25 vs Jake's 15 (+10 for Mike), Mike's 35 vs Jake's 45 (−10 for Mike), Mike's 7 vs Jake's 3 (+4 for Mike). In total Mike is $10 - 10 + 4 = 4$ points ahead.

**Answer: (E)**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-07.title: Continue the checkerboard
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-07.body:
Grey and striped tiles alternate in every row and every column, like a chessboard. Fill in the hole row by row:

- Row 2: two tiles are missing; the first one is grey → 1 grey.
- Row 3: five tiles are missing: grey, striped, grey, striped, grey → 3 grey.
- Row 4: six tiles are missing: grey, striped, grey, striped, grey, striped → 3 grey.

$1 + 3 + 3 = 7$.

**Answer: (C) 7**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-07.title: Count all and subtract
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-07.body:
The wall is 8 tiles long and 5 tiles high: 40 tiles. In a chessboard pattern half of them, 20, are grey. Counting the grey tiles still on the wall gives 13, so $20 - 13 = 7$ grey tiles fell off.

**Answer: (C) 7**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-08.title: Count the days in two parts
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-08.body:
From 24 February to 29 February: $29 - 24 = 5$ days. Then from 29 February to 15 March: 15 days. Total $5 + 15 = 20$ days.

**Answer: (D) 20 days**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-08.title: Count back from 15 March
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-08.body:
15 days back from 15 March is the last day of February (29 February). The chicks hatched 5 days before that (25, 26, 27, 28, 29 February → 24 February). $15 + 5 = 20$ days.

**Answer: (D) 20 days**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-09.title: Split each shape
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-09.body:
Try to cut every shape into two L pieces of 4 squares:

- The 2 × 4 rectangle: an L standing up on the left and an upside-down L on the right fit together.
- The second shape: the left column of 3 with the bottom square next to it is one L; the middle column of 3 with the square sticking out on the right is the other.
- The third shape: the top row of 3 with the square below its left end is one L; the column of 3 below with the square at the bottom right is the other.
- The fourth shape: the top 3 squares of the tall column with the square to the right of the third one form one L; the bottom row of 3 with the square above its right end is the other.

All **4** shapes work.

**Answer: (E) 4**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-09.title: Each shape is two Ls
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-09.body:
All four shapes have 8 squares, which is right for two Ls. Turning and flipping an L allowed, you can find an L of 4 squares in each shape such that the 4 squares left over also form an L. Since none of the shapes fails, the answer is all 4.

**Answer: (E) 4**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-10.title: Two extra balloons
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-10.body:
3 balloons are 2 balloons more than 1 balloon. So 2 balloons cost 12 cents, and 1 balloon costs $12 \div 2 = 6$ cents.

**Answer: (B) 6 cents**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-10.title: Check the choices
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-10.body:
If a balloon costs 6 cents: 3 balloons cost 18 cents, and $18 - 6 = 12$. ✓

**Answer: (B) 6 cents**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-11.title: Count the extra decorations
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-11.body:
$15 + 15 = 30$ decorations went on 20 biscuits. Every biscuit got at least one. The $30 - 20 = 10$ extra decorations are on biscuits that got both.

**Answer: (E) 10**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-11.title: Biscuits without raisins
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-11.body:
$20 - 15 = 5$ biscuits got no raisins, so they must have nuts (none is left over). The other $15 - 5 = 10$ biscuits with nuts also have raisins.

**Answer: (E) 10**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-12.title: Subtract the known legs
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-12.body:
Cats: $3 \times 4 = 12$, ducks: $2 \times 2 = 4$, sheep: $2 \times 4 = 8$. Together 24 legs. The dogs have $44 - 24 = 20$ legs, so there are $20 \div 4 = 5$ dogs.

**Answer: (B) 5**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-13.title: Find all 12 cubes
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-13.body:
The block is 2 cubes wide, 3 deep and 2 high: 12 cubes, 4 of each colour.

- Light grey we can see: both front top cubes, the front bottom right cube and the middle bottom right cube → 4.
- Dark grey we can see: the back top row, the middle top right cube and the back bottom right cube → 4.
- White we can see: the front bottom left cube and the middle top left cube. The other two white cubes must be the hidden ones: middle bottom left and back bottom left.

So the white piece is a row of 3 cubes (bottom left, front to back) with one cube on top of the middle one.

**Answer: (D)**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-13.title: Rule out the others
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-13.body:
The white piece contains the front bottom left cube and the cube on top of the middle left position, so it has a cube sitting on top of the middle of a row of three. (A), (B), (C) and (E) do not have that shape; (D) does.

**Answer: (D)**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-14.title: Two groups of tables
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-14.body:
$6 \times 5 = 30$ plates. The other $15 - 6 = 9$ tables get $9 \times 3 = 27$ plates. Total $30 + 27 = 57$.

**Answer: (C) 57**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-14.title: Start with 3 everywhere
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-14.body:
Put 3 plates on all 15 tables: 45 plates. The 6 big tables need 2 more each: $6 \times 2 = 12$. Total $45 + 12 = 57$.

**Answer: (C) 57**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-15.title: Up and down jumps
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-15.body:
Going only up: 3, 6, 9, 12, ... never hits 10. Every down jump takes away 4, so we need $3 \times (\text{up}) - 4 \times (\text{down}) = 10$.

- 1 down jump: up jumps must give 14 — not a multiple of 3.
- 2 down jumps: up jumps must give 18 = 6 jumps of 3. ✓

That is $6 + 2 = 8$ jumps, e.g. 3, 6, 9, 12, 8, 11, 14, 10.

**Answer: (E) 8**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-15.title: Look at the remainders
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-15.body:
After 1, 2, 3, ... up jumps you are on step 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18. A down jump changes the step by 4. From 18, two down jumps reach 10. Fewer up jumps don't work: from 12 you would reach 8 or 4, from 15 you reach 11 or 7. So the fewest jumps is $6 + 2 = 8$.

**Answer: (E) 8**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-16.title: Add what you can see
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-16.body:
The visible dominoes are 1|0, 0|5, 5|3, 3|2 and 1|2, with $1 + 0 + 0 + 5 + 5 + 3 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 2 = 22$ points. The two missing dominoes have $33 - 22 = 11$ points.

Because touching halves match, they are 2|? and ?|1. So $2 + ? + ? + 1 = 11$, which means $? + ? = 8$ and $? = 4$.

**Answer: (C) 4**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-16.title: Check
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-16.body:
With ? = 4 the missing dominoes are 2|4 and 4|1: $2 + 4 + 4 + 1 = 11$, and $22 + 11 = 33$. ✓

**Answer: (C) 4**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-17.title: Work out the calculations first
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-17.body:
The grid becomes:

- Row 1: 1, _, 3, _
- Row 2: 4, 3, _, 1
- Row 3: 3, 4, 1, _
- Row 4: 2, 1, _, grey

Column 3 already has 3 and 1, row 2 needs a 2 there, so row 4 column 3 is 4. Row 4 then has 2, 1, 4, so the grey square is **3**.

**Answer: (C) 3**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-17.title: Use the last column
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-17.body:
Last column: row 2 is 1. Row 3 has 3, 4, 1, so its last cell is 2. Row 1 has 1 and 3 and its second cell must be 2 (column 2 has 3, 4, 1), so row 1 ends with 4. Column 4 now has 4, 1, 2 — the grey cell is 3.

**Answer: (C) 3**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-18.title: Don't forget Thomas
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-18.body:
Thomas's classmates are everyone except Thomas. Among them, for every boy there are 2 girls, so the number of classmates is a multiple of 3 (1 + 2 = 3). The whole class is classmates **plus Thomas**: a multiple of 3, plus 1.

- 30, 24: multiples of 3 (no).
- 20 → 19 classmates, 29 → 28 classmates: not multiples of 3.
- 25 → 24 classmates = 8 boys + 16 girls. ✓

**Answer: (D) 25**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-18.title: Build a class
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-18.body:
Try 8 boy classmates and 16 girl classmates. With Thomas there are $8 + 16 + 1 = 25$ children. No other choice is "one more than a multiple of 3".

**Answer: (D) 25**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-19.title: Biggest digits in the biggest places
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-19.body:
The hundreds digits count 100 times, so use 6 and 5 there. Then 4 and 3 for the tens, and 2 and 1 for the ones: e.g. $642 + 531 = 1173$.

**Answer: (D) 1173**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-19.title: Place values
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-19.body:
Sum $= 100 \times (6+5) + 10 \times (4+3) + (2+1) = 1100 + 70 + 3 = 1173$. 1221 is impossible because the hundreds can give at most 1100 and the rest at most $70 + 3$.

**Answer: (D) 1173**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-20.title: Anna in the middle of a group
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-20.body:
Anna needs Katharina and Lisa both next to her, so the three stand as Lisa–Anna–Katharina or Katharina–Anna–Lisa. Laura stands on the left or on the right of this group: $2 \times 2 = 4$ ways.

**Answer: (B) 4**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-20.title: List them
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-20.body:
With L = Laura, S = Lisa, A = Anna, K = Katharina:

- L S A K
- L K A S
- S A K L
- K A S L

4 ways.

**Answer: (B) 4**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-21.title: Find out which hand is which
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-21.body:
At 12:55:30: the second hand points at 6 (30 seconds), the minute hand points just past 11 (55 minutes), and the hour hand is almost at 1. In the picture, the short hand pointing down is the second hand, the hand pointing to 11 is the minute hand and the hand near 1 is the hour hand.

At 8:11:00: the second hand (short) points at 12, the minute hand points just past 2 (11 minutes), and the hour hand points just past 8. Only picture (E) shows this.

**Answer: (E)**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-21.title: Rule out pictures
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-21.body:
At 8:11:00 the seconds are 0, so the hand that was at 6 must point straight up at 12, and one hand must point a bit past 2 (11 minutes) with the hand that was near 1 pointing at about 8. The longest hand (the minute hand, at 11 in the first picture) must point a bit past 2. In (A) and (C) the longest hand points at 8, and in (B) the long hand points at 12. In (D) the hand pointing towards 8 is too short — it should be the medium-length hour hand. (E) fits.

**Answer: (E)**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-23.title: Cut step by step
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-23.body:
- 60 × 36: cut a 36 × 36 square, left 24 × 36.
- 24 × 36: cut a 24 × 24 square, left 24 × 12.
- 24 × 12: cut a 12 × 12 square, left 12 × 12 — a square!

**Answer: (E) 12 mm**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-23.title: Common measure
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-23.body:
Each cut takes the shorter side away from the longer one, so both sides stay multiples of any length that measures both 60 and 36. The biggest length that divides both 60 and 36 is 12, and the process ends exactly there.

**Answer: (E) 12 mm**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-24.title: Win as much as possible
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-24.body:
To lose many games, the team should get its 80 points in as few games as possible, so it should win as often as it can. $26 \times 3 = 78$, and 2 draws add 2 points: 80 points in $26 + 2 = 28$ games. The other $36 - 28 = 8$ games were lost.

(27 wins would be 81 points — too many.)

**Answer: (E) 8**

kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-24.title: Check a bigger number
kangaroo-at-2012-ecolier-24.body:
Could the team lose 9 games? Then 80 points come from 27 games. Even 27 wins give 81 and any draw instead of a win loses 2 points, giving 79, 77, ... — never 80. So 8 is the maximum.

**Answer: (E) 8**
